# Runtime Enforcement for Agents: Tetragon, OpenTelemetry, and nono

Put production tools in charge of the sandbox. Write Tetragon policies that observe, then kill, a coding agent's credential reads and outbound connections; route every event through an OpenTelemetry collector; drop the agent's privileges with setpriv and build a Landlock sandbox by hand; then confine the same agent with nono so the paths and ports it may not touch stop existing at all.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

This lab runs its agent on a local Ollama model. The Zenable sandbox has the model already downloaded and built; take the hosted version at https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme.

**Duration** 70 minutes · **Difficulty** Advanced

**Topics** `Security` · `Guardrails & Policy` · `Observability`

**Prerequisites**

- Familiarity with system calls and eBPF hooks
- Docker and git
- Comfort reading YAML and JSON
- A Linux kernel 6.7 or newer with BTF. Your sandbox has one; the Getting started section checks

---

_This README is only the hands-on lab. The concept walk-through (You wouldn't ship the program you wrote last time · Terminology · Putting it together · Conclusion) lives on the [Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=agent-runtime-enforcement&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme)._

## Getting started

_~5 min · Hands-on_

Clone the repository and check the kernel. Tetragon needs BTF; nono's port filtering needs Landlock ABI 4, which is kernel 6.7:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
  || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement
uv sync --locked
uname -r
cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm; echo
ls -la /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux
```

```console
$ cd ~
$ git clone https://github.com/Zenable-io/labs.git ~/zenable-labs 2>/dev/null \
>   || git -C ~/zenable-labs pull --ff-only
$ cd ~/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement
$ uv sync --locked
$ uname -r
7.2.6-1.el8.elrepo.x86_64
$ cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm; echo
lockdown,capability,landlock,yama,selinux,bpf,ima,evm
$ ls -la /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux
-r--r--r--. 1 root root 5418291 Nov  8 15:21 /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux
```

Our agent is goose, driving a local `qwen3-nothink` model through a three-step task that reads a decoy credential file and fetches a URL. Your sandbox comes with both.

<details>
<summary>Not using the Zenable sandboxes?</summary>

Install goose, pinned to the version this lab was written against. The installer needs `bzip2` and `tar`, and puts goose in `~/.local/bin`, so also add that directory to the `PATH` in your shell profile for new terminals to find it:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/releases/download/stable/download_cli.sh | CONFIGURE=false GOOSE_VERSION=v1.53.0 bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Download the model. Run this on its own and wait for it to finish, because the progress display takes over the terminal and swallows anything you paste behind it:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
```

Then build a copy of it with thinking pinned off. It reuses the weights already on disk, so there's no download and it finishes in about a second:

```bash
ollama show --modelfile qwen3:1.7b > Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|^FROM /.*|FROM qwen3:1.7b|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if and $.IsThinkSet (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|{{- if (eq $i $lastUserIdx) }}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{- if $.Think -}}|{{- if false -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
sed -i 's|{{ if and $.IsThinkSet (not $.Think) -}}|{{ if true -}}|' Modelfile.nothink
grep -q '{{ if true -}}' Modelfile.nothink
ollama create qwen3-nothink -f Modelfile.nothink
```

> [!NOTE]
> If you want more on what each line does, see the [Syscalls and seccomp](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=syscalls-and-seccomp&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=agent-runtime-enforcement_readme) lab.

</details>

Let's check that both answer:

```bash
goose --version
ollama run qwen3-nothink "Reply with only the word: pong"
```

```console
$ goose --version
 1.53.0
$ ollama run qwen3-nothink "Reply with only the word: pong"
pong
```

Tetragon matches processes by the absolute path of their binary, and goose's path depends on how it was installed, so the policies ship as templates. Render them for this machine, then start Tetragon and the collector:

```bash
./scripts/render-policies.sh
docker compose up -d --wait
./scripts/wait-for-tetragon.sh
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
```

```console
$ ./scripts/render-policies.sh
rendered 10-observe.yaml for /usr/local/bin/goose
rendered 20-enforce.yaml for /usr/local/bin/goose
$ docker compose up -d --wait
$ ./scripts/wait-for-tetragon.sh
tetragon is answering, agent-observe enabled
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
ID   NAME            STATE     FILTERID   NAMESPACE   SENSORS          KERNELMEMORY   MODE           NPOST   NENFORCE   NMONITOR
2    agent-observe   enabled   0          (global)    generic_kprobe   765.46 kB      monitor_only   0       0          0
```

Two containers, and a short wait: `compose up --wait` returns when the container is running, which for Tetragon is a few seconds before its API answers and its startup policy has finished loading. The wait script holds on until the policy reports `enabled`, because adding or deleting a policy while another is still loading can take Tetragon down. Tetragon runs privileged with the host's pid namespace and this kernel's BTF mounted in, which is what it needs to attach to the same hooks you attached to by hand. The collector tails the JSON export file Tetragon writes. One policy is loaded, the observe one; the enforce one sits rendered beside it until we add it by hand.

## Finding the LSM hooks

_~4 min · Hands-on_

Both halves of this lab end at the same place inside the kernel, so let's look at it before the tools cover it up. Getting started printed `lockdown,capability,landlock,yama,selinux,bpf,ima,evm`: the security modules this kernel loaded, in the order it asks them. Each module answers at a fixed set of points, and those points are ordinary kernel functions with `security_` in front of their name. Let's count them and find the four this lab lands on:

```bash
grep -cE ' [Tt] security_' /proc/kallsyms
grep -E ' [Tt] security_(file_open|file_permission|socket_connect|capable)$' /proc/kallsyms
```

```console
$ grep -cE ' [Tt] security_' /proc/kallsyms
342
$ grep -E ' [Tt] security_(file_open|file_permission|socket_connect|capable)$' /proc/kallsyms
0000000000000000 T security_capable
0000000000000000 T security_file_permission
0000000000000000 T security_file_open
0000000000000000 T security_socket_connect
```

Now let's watch one of them fire for an open we type ourselves:

```bash
sudo bpftrace -e 'kprobe:security_file_open /comm == "cat"/ { printf("%s opened %s\n", comm, str(((struct file *)arg0)->f_path.dentry->d_name.name)); }' -c '/usr/bin/cat decoys/.aws/credentials'
```

```console
cat opened ld.so.cache
cat opened libc-2.28.so
cat opened locale-archive
cat opened credentials
# Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc. DECOY. Nothing here is a real credential; the lab watches who reads it.
[default]
aws_access_key_id = DECOY0000000000000000
aws_secret_access_key = decoy/not/a/secret/just/a/canary/for/this/lab
```

Every `opened` line is the kernel pausing at `security_file_open`, with the file already resolved, and asking the list for a verdict. `cat` printed the decoy afterwards because no module had a rule about that file. Tetragon's observe policy, already loaded, hooks `security_file_permission`, one of these functions. A Landlock ruleset is what the `landlock` module answers from at `security_file_open`. And `bpf` in the list is what lets an eBPF program return the verdict here itself.

## Observe

_~7 min · Hands-on_

Open `policies/10-observe.yaml.tmpl`. It hooks two kernel functions, and both times the selector starts by scoping to goose and everything goose spawns:

```yaml
spec:
  kprobes:
  - call: security_file_permission
    syscall: false
    return: true
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: file
    - index: 1
      type: int   # 0x04 is MAY_READ, 0x02 is MAY_WRITE
    selectors:
    - matchBinaries:
      - operator: In
        followChildren: true
        values:
        - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
      matchArgs:
      - index: 0
        operator: Postfix
        values:
        - "/.aws/credentials"
      - index: 1
        operator: Equal
        values:
        - "4"
  - call: tcp_connect
    syscall: false
    args:
    - index: 0
      type: sock
    selectors:
    - matchBinaries:
      - operator: In
        followChildren: true
        values:
        - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
```

Compare this to last lab's C. `followChildren: true` is the `ProcessTree` you wrote, `type: file` is `bpf_d_path`, and `Postfix` on the path is the credential scan. `security_file_permission` is an LSM hook that runs on every read and write with the file already resolved, which is why the policy can match a path rather than a syscall argument. `tcp_connect` is the kernel function under every outbound TCP connection, with the socket decoded so the destination is right there.

Start reading events in a second terminal. `-o compact` is one line per event:

```bash
docker compose exec tetragon tetra getevents -o compact
```

Back in the first terminal, run the agent:

```bash
./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
```

Your second terminal fills up as it runs. The lines that matter:

```console
$ grep -E '📚 read|🔌 connect' tetra.out | head -10
```

Success! A `read` of the credentials by `cat`, with goose as the ancestor that makes it match, and a `connect` from `curl` to port 443 plus the model calls to `127.0.0.1:11434`. Nothing from any other process on the machine, because `matchBinaries` filtered in the kernel before the event was ever written.

There's one `connect` we didn't ask for, though: goose itself, to port 443, before the model has even been called. Since 1.53.0 goose refreshes its model catalog from `models.dev` every time it starts ([goose#12560](https://github.com/aaif-goose/goose/pull/12560)), falling back to the copy it ships with when that fails. Keep it in mind; it matters in the next section.

> [!TIP]
> **Pro Tip: Watch again after every upgrade**
> When we update this lab, we often catch new network activity. In 1.53.0, goose started checking its model catalog on every startup, and our enforce policy killed it before it ever reached the task. That's exactly what the policy is there for, so whenever you upgrade an agent, run the observe policy again and see what's new.

Question: the policy watches `security_file_permission` rather than the `openat` syscall you hooked last lab. What does that buy, and what does it cost? Have a guess before opening the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

It buys the path. A syscall hook sees whatever string the caller passed, so `../../decoys/.aws/credentials` and a symlink both dodge a match on the literal path; the LSM hook sees the resolved file. It also fires on every read, not just the open, so a file descriptor handed across a fork is still caught. The cost is volume: `security_file_permission` fires for every read on the machine, and Tetragon's in-kernel filtering is the only reason that's affordable. A policy with a weak selector on this hook is how you learn what "eBPF overhead" means.

</details>

## Enforce

_~8 min · Hands-on_

`policies/20-enforce.yaml.tmpl` is the observe policy with actions added. The credential read gets a `Sigkill`, and the connect gets one too, but only for destinations off loopback, so the model on `127.0.0.1:11434` stays reachable:

```yaml
selectors:
- matchBinaries:
  - operator: In
    values:
    - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
  matchArgs:
  - index: 0
    operator: DPort
    values:
    - "443"
- matchBinaries:
  - operator: In
    followChildren: true
    values:
    - "${GOOSE_BIN}"
  matchArgs:
  - index: 0
    operator: NotDAddr
    values:
    - 127.0.0.0/8
    - ::1/128
  matchActions:
  - action: Sigkill
```

The second selector is a rule seccomp can't express, because a seccomp filter sees the syscall number and can't follow the pointer to the destination address: anything in the agent's tree that connects off loopback dies. On its own, though, it kills goose itself the moment it starts, because of that catalog refresh you saw in Observe. goose never gets as far as the task.

That's what the first selector is for. Tetragon applies only the first selector that matches, and this one names goose without `followChildren`, so it matches goose's own process and nothing it spawns. It has no action, which means Tetragon reports the connect and lets it through. A `curl` that goose runs doesn't match it and falls through to the kill.

Question: the first selector trusts goose's own HTTPS to anywhere, not just to `models.dev`. Why can't the policy name the host instead? Have a guess before opening the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`tcp_connect` sees an address and a port. By the time the kernel connects anything, the hostname has already been resolved to an IP, and `models.dev` sits behind a CDN whose addresses change and are shared with thousands of other sites. Pinning a host takes something that sees the name, like an egress proxy or DNS-aware policy on the host. In this lab, the closest we get is nono, later on, which can block the network outright and open single ports.

</details>

Swap the policies: remove observe, add enforce. Tetragon loads and unloads them live:

```bash
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-observe
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
```

```console
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-observe
tracing policy "agent-observe" deleted
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
tracing policy "/policies/20-enforce.yaml" added
$ docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy list
ID   NAME            STATE     FILTERID   NAMESPACE   SENSORS          KERNELMEMORY   MODE      NPOST   NENFORCE   NMONITOR
3    agent-enforce   enabled   0          (global)    generic_kprobe   765.46 kB      enforce   0       0          0
```

Run the agent again with the event stream open in the other terminal:

```bash
./run-agent.sh > agent-enforce.out 2>&1
```

```console
$ grep -E '📚 read|🔌 connect|💥 exit' tetra-enforce.out | head -10
```

Two `💥 exit … SIGKILL` lines: `cat` died on the credential read and `curl` died on the connect. goose itself carried on, reported both steps as failed, and its model calls to loopback went through untouched, as did its catalog refresh on port 443. One policy, kernel-enforced, that names the file and the destination.

Now the caveat you already know from last lab. `Sigkill` is a signal, and the read that triggered it had already returned by the time the signal landed. Look at what `cat` managed to print into goose's transcript:

```bash
grep -c DECOY agent-enforce.out || true
```

```console
0
```

Sometimes zero, sometimes one, depending on whether `cat` wrote its output before the signal arrived. Tetragon's docs are direct about this: `Sigkill` "does not always stop the operation being performed by the process that triggered the operation", and the fix is to pair it with an `Override` action, which uses the kernel's error injection to make the hooked function return an error before it runs. That works on security hooks and system calls, on kernels built with `CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE`. Add it to the credential selector:

```yaml
matchActions:
- action: Override
  argError: -1
- action: Sigkill
```

<details>
<summary>Try it</summary>

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("policies/rendered/20-enforce.yaml")
text = p.read_text()
marker = "      matchActions:\n      - action: Sigkill\n  - call: tcp_connect"
assert marker in text
p.write_text(text.replace(marker, "      matchActions:\n      - action: Override\n        argError: -1\n      - action: Sigkill\n  - call: tcp_connect"))
EOF
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy delete agent-enforce
docker compose exec tetragon tetra tracingpolicy add /policies/20-enforce.yaml
./run-agent.sh > agent-override.out 2>&1
grep -c DECOY agent-override.out || true
```

Zero, every time: the read returned `EPERM` and never produced bytes to print. The kernel decided instead of reacting, exactly the LSM hook you wrote by hand, expressed as two lines of YAML.

</details>

## The pipeline

_~6 min · Hands-on_

Everything `tetra getevents` showed you also went to a JSON file, and the collector has been tailing it the whole time. Its config parses each line and stamps the event kind as an attribute:

```yaml
file_log/tetragon:
  include: [/var/log/tetragon/tetragon.log]
  operators:
    - type: json_parser
      parse_to: attributes
    - type: add
      field: attributes.tetragon.event
      value: 'EXPR(keys(attributes)[0])'
```

Read the collector's output for the kill:

```bash
docker compose logs collector > collector.log 2>&1
grep -c 'LogRecord #' collector.log
grep -A20 'process_kprobe' collector.log | grep -E 'binary|SIGKILL|dport' | sed -n '1,8p'
```

The same events, now as log records with attributes, with `service.name: tetragon` on the resource. Beside them sit the records from last lab's hand-written watcher, if you left that collector running, and the two streams describe the same facts with the same vocabulary. Point the `debug` exporter at an OTLP backend and this is a real feed.

<details>
<summary>Stretch: trace the agent's model calls with zero code</summary>

[OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/) attaches to a running process from outside and emits HTTP spans without touching its code. `compose.yaml` carries it under a profile, targeting the goose binary and exporting to the same collector:

```bash
docker compose --profile obi up -d --wait
./run-agent.sh >/dev/null
docker compose logs obi > obi.log 2>&1
grep -E 'POST /api' obi.log | head -5
```

Each goose turn is a `POST /api/chat` span to Ollama, with duration, status and the peer, next to the kernel events for the same process. That's the model layer and the kernel layer in one stream, which is where an agent's story actually lives.

</details>

## Dropping privileges with setpriv

_~6 min · Hands-on_

Everything so far watched the agent. Before we confine it, let's take away what it never needed. On this sandbox your user has passwordless `sudo`, and an agent you run inherits that, so let's confirm what the agent starts with:

```bash
sudo -n id -u
grep -E 'NoNewPrivs|CapBnd|CapEff' /proc/self/status
```

```console
$ sudo -n id -u
0
$ grep -E 'NoNewPrivs|CapBnd|CapEff' /proc/self/status
CapEff:	0000000000000000
CapBnd:	000001ffffffffff
NoNewPrivs:	0
```

`sudo` answers as root, and `NoNewPrivs` is 0: this process may still gain privilege by running a setuid binary. `setpriv`, from util-linux, changes exactly those things about a process before it execs the command you give it. The one flag any user may set is `--nnp`, which turns on `no_new_privs`:

```bash
setpriv --nnp -- sudo -n id -u
```

```console
sudo: effective uid is not 0, is /usr/bin/sudo on a file system with the 'nosuid' option set or an NFS file system without root privileges?
```

The setuid bit on `sudo` stopped meaning anything, and the kernel never turns `no_new_privs` back off, in this process or any child it starts. Let's check what the bit left alone:

```bash
setpriv --nnp -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
```

```console
# Copyright (c) 2026 Zenable, Inc. DECOY. Nothing here is a real credential; the lab watches who reads it.
[default]
aws_access_key_id = DECOY0000000000000000
aws_secret_access_key = decoy/not/a/secret/just/a/canary/for/this/lab
```

The credential file prints in full. `no_new_privs` is about what a process can *become*: with it set, exec ignores setuid bits and file capabilities, so nothing this process starts is ever more privileged than it is. It says nothing about what the process can *reach*, and every file your user can read, this process can read too. Now the agent itself, asked to do the one thing we just took away:

```bash
setpriv --nnp -- ./run-agent.sh "Run this shell command and report its exact output: sudo -n id -u" 2>&1 | tail -6
```

```console
$ setpriv --nnp -- ./run-agent.sh "Run this shell command and report its exact output: sudo -n id -u" 2>&1 | tail -6
```

Shrinking the capability bounding set takes `CAP_SETPCAP`, which your user doesn't hold, so the fuller form runs through `sudo` and comes straight back down to you with nothing:

```bash
sudo setpriv --reuid "$(id -u)" --regid "$(id -g)" --init-groups \
  --bounding-set -all --inh-caps -all --ambient-caps -all --nnp \
  -- grep -E 'NoNewPrivs|CapBnd|CapEff' /proc/self/status
```

```console
$ sudo setpriv --reuid "$(id -u)" --regid "$(id -g)" --init-groups \
>   --bounding-set -all --inh-caps -all --ambient-caps -all --nnp \
>   -- grep -E 'NoNewPrivs|CapBnd|CapEff' /proc/self/status
CapEff:	0000000000000000
CapBnd:	0000000000000000
NoNewPrivs:	1
```

`CapBnd` is all zeros: no binary this process execs can ever hold a capability, whatever bits are set on its file. That's the launcher pattern container runtimes use, privileged for a moment to drop everything, then exec as you. The check itself happens in the LSM list you counted: when a process asks for a capability, `security_capable` goes down the list and `capability`, first in it, reads the sets you just emptied. Newer util-linux lets `setpriv` apply Landlock rules and a seccomp filter in the same breath (`--landlock-access`, `--seccomp-filter`); Rocky 8 ships 2.32, which has neither, so the next section builds the Landlock half by hand.

## Landlock by hand

_~8 min · Hands-on_

`landlock.py` is Landlock with nothing in between: three system calls, made through `ctypes`, then an exec. Let's start by asking the kernel what it offers:

```bash
uv run python landlock.py --show
```

```console
Landlock ABI 10
handled rights (0xffff): execute, write_file, read_file, read_dir, remove_dir, remove_file, make_char, make_dir, make_reg, make_sock, make_fifo, make_block, make_sym, refer, truncate, ioctl_dev
```

The ABI number is how a program finds out which rights this kernel can police; the script asks, then handles every right the kernel knows, because an unhandled right is one the sandbox silently permits. Here's the part that does the work:

```python
handled = handled_access(abi)
ruleset_fd = create_ruleset(handled)
for path in args.read:
    add_path(ruleset_fd, path, READ_RIGHTS)
for path in args.allow:
    add_path(ruleset_fd, path, handled)
restrict_self(ruleset_fd)
os.execvp(args.command[0], args.command)
```

Now let's grant the workspace and the system paths a binary needs to start, and read a file inside the grant:

```bash
uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- cat workspace/VERSION
```

```console
2026.09.15
```

Then the decoy, which no grant names, first directly and then from a shell that starts another shell:

```bash
uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- sh -c 'sh -c "cat decoys/.aws/credentials"'
```

```console
$ uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
cat: decoys/.aws/credentials: Permission denied
$ uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- sh -c 'sh -c "cat decoys/.aws/credentials"'
cat: decoys/.aws/credentials: Permission denied
```

The file is readable by your user; the process just has no grant that reaches it. And the restriction travels into every child, so a shell inside the sandbox starting another shell changes nothing.

Landlock decides at `security_file_open`, after the kernel has resolved the path, so let's try to reach the decoy through a name that sits inside the grant:

```bash
ln -sfn ../decoys/.aws/credentials workspace/notes.txt
uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- cat workspace/notes.txt
```

```console
$ ln -sfn ../decoys/.aws/credentials workspace/notes.txt
$ uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc -- cat workspace/notes.txt
cat: workspace/notes.txt: Permission denied
```

Denied, with the same error. The name we typed is inside `workspace`, and a check on the string would have let it through. By the time `security_file_open` runs, the kernel has followed the link, and the `landlock` module sees the decoy's file with no grant that reaches it.

Question: `/usr` was granted read-only, so how did `cat` start at all? Have a guess before opening the answer 🤔

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Landlock's read grant in this script is three rights together: `read_file`, `read_dir` and `execute`. The `cat` binary and the libraries it loads live under `/usr`, so executing them is covered. A grant of `read_file` alone would have let the sandbox read `/usr/bin/cat` as data and refused to run it.

</details>

Let's look at one more thing the sandbox changed about the process, with `/proc` added to the grant so it can read its status:

```bash
uv run python landlock.py --allow workspace --read /usr --read /lib --read /lib64 --read /etc --read /proc -- grep NoNewPrivs /proc/self/status
```

```console
NoNewPrivs:	1
```

`NoNewPrivs` is 1, and `landlock.py` is what set it, on the `prctl` line in `restrict_self`. `landlock_restrict_self` refuses to enforce a ruleset for a process that could still gain privilege; the [man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/landlock_restrict_self.2.html) says this "avoids scenarios where unprivileged processes can affect the behavior of privileged children (e.g., because of set-user-ID binaries)", the same rule seccomp has. So the bit and the ruleset arrive together in every sandbox built this way. They still do different jobs:

| | `no_new_privs` | Landlock |
|---|---|---|
| Restricts | becoming more: setuid bits and file capabilities at exec | reaching more: paths and ports |
| Shape | one bit, set once | a ruleset, built per process |
| Checked | at exec, in the credential code | at every open and connect, in the LSM hooks |
| Leaves alone | every file you could already read | your uid and your capabilities |
| Needs | nothing | the bit, or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` |

Success! 🎉 A process we started as our own user, with no root anywhere, now sees a filesystem where the decoy doesn't exist. nono, next, is this same ruleset built from a profile instead of flags, with a network proxy beside it.

## nono

_~10 min · Hands-on_

Tetragon watches and reacts. nono restricts first. Install it, pinned and checksum-verified:

```bash
./scripts/install-nono.sh
```

```console
nono-v0.79.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz: OK
nono 0.79.0
```

Before running anything, ask nono what it would grant. `--dry-run -v` prints the Landlock ruleset and the ABI level the kernel offers:

```bash
nono run --dry-run -v --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh > dry-run.txt 2>&1
grep -E 'Landlock|net |ipc |zenable-labs' dry-run.txt
```

```console
$ nono run --dry-run -v --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh > dry-run.txt 2>&1
$ grep -E 'Landlock|net |ipc |zenable-labs' dry-run.txt
   r+w  /home/as2-streaming-user/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/dry-run.txt (file) [group:system_read_linux_core]
   r+w  /home/as2-streaming-user/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement (dir) [user]
   net  outbound blocked
   ipc  localhost:11434
   scope  Landlock V6 detected
2026-11-09T20:22:50.294554Z  INFO Landlock available (Landlock V6, features: Basic filesystem access control, File rename across directories (Refer), File truncation (Truncate), TCP network filtering, Device ioctl filtering, Signal and abstract UNIX socket scoping)
```

`Landlock V6 detected` means every rule can be applied on this kernel. The grants are the checkout, read-write, plus the system paths every process needs; the network is blocked and one localhost port is opened back up, 11434, for the model. Nothing else exists. Now the agent for real:

```bash
nono run --no-rollback --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

```console
$ nono run --no-rollback --allow "$PWD" --block-net --open-port 11434 -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

Hmm, the credential read went through. `--allow "$PWD"` granted the whole checkout, and `decoys/` is inside it. That's the first thing to understand about a path allowlist: it's exactly as good as the paths you list. nono has a default deny list for the usual credential locations under your home directory, but a decoy inside the working directory isn't on it. And the fetch failed, this time not with a refused connection: with Landlock the socket can't be created towards that destination at all, so `curl` reports the failure at the network layer before any packet leaves.

Use the profile in the repository instead. It grants `workspace/` and `goose/` and never mentions `decoys/`, blocks the network and opens only port 11434, and passes only the home, executable path, locale and terminal settings into the child. Our model runs locally, so it needs none of the cloud credentials a shared coding agent sandbox may export. Landlock is an allow-list, so there is no denying a path inside a directory you granted; the checkout is granted piece by piece and the decoys are what's left out. The paths assume the checkout is under `$HOME/zenable-labs`; adjust them if yours lives elsewhere:

```jsonc
{
  "meta": {
    "name": "agent",
    "description": "goose, confined to the lab checkout and its local model"
  },
  "filesystem": {
    "read": ["$HOME/.local/bin"],
    "read_file": ["$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/run-agent.sh"],
    "allow": [
      "$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/workspace",
      "$HOME/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/goose"
    ]
  },
  "network": {
    "block": true,
    "open_port": [11434]
  },
  "environment": {
    "allow_vars": ["HOME", "PATH", "LANG", "TERM"]
  }
}
```

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/nono/profiles
cp nono/agent.jsonc ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono profile validate ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono why --profile agent --path "$PWD/decoys/.aws/credentials" --op read
nono why --profile agent --host example.com --port 443
```

```console
$ mkdir -p ~/.config/nono/profiles
$ cp nono/agent.jsonc ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
$ nono profile validate ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
nono profile: validating /home/as2-streaming-user/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc

  [ok]  JSON syntax valid
  [ok]  All 18 group references valid

  Result: valid
$ nono why --profile agent --path "$PWD/decoys/.aws/credentials" --op read
DENIED
  Reason: path_not_granted
  Details: Path is not covered by any capability: /home/as2-streaming-user/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/decoys/.aws/credentials
  Suggested fix: --read-file /home/as2-streaming-user/zenable-labs/labs/agent-runtime-enforcement/decoys/.aws/credentials
$ nono why --profile agent --host example.com --port 443
DENIED
  Reason: network_blocked
  Details: Network access is fully blocked. Connection to example.com:443 would be denied.
  Suggested fix: --allow-domain example.com
```

`nono why` answers the policy question from the profile alone, without starting the agent, which is the tool you want when a profile grows past a screen. Now the agent under the profile. `--workdir` tells nono where the agent runs, since a profile carries no working directory of its own:

```bash
nono run --no-rollback --profile agent --workdir "$PWD" -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

```console
$ nono run --no-rollback --profile agent --workdir "$PWD" -- ./run-agent.sh 2>&1 | tail -12
```

Success! `cat` got `Permission denied` on the credentials, `curl` couldn't even resolve example.com, and goose still talked to its model. No race, no signal, no event to react to, because from inside the sandbox those two things were never possible. And nono kept a record:

```bash
nono audit list --command run-agent.sh | head -8
```

```console
$ nono audit list --command run-agent.sh | head -8
```

The Python wrapper reads the same environment allowlist from the profile, with environment inheritance disabled. `nono_agent.py` builds the capability set in code, blocks the network entirely, and runs a command in a sandboxed child while the parent stays free, with `enforcement_mode="seccomp"`, which layers a static seccomp filter under Landlock so that even the socket types Landlock doesn't cover are denied:

```python
caps = CapabilitySet()
caps.allow_path(str(HERE / "workspace"), AccessMode.READ_WRITE)
caps.allow_path(str(HERE / "goose"), AccessMode.READ_WRITE)
for system in ("/usr", "/lib", "/lib64", "/etc", str(Path.home() / ".local" / "bin")):
    if Path(system).exists():
        caps.allow_path(system, AccessMode.READ)
caps.block_network()

result = sandboxed_exec(caps, command, cwd=str(HERE), timeout_secs=args.timeout,
                        env=child_environment(), inherit_env=False,
                        enforcement_mode=args.mode)
```

```bash
uv run python nono_agent.py -- cat decoys/.aws/credentials
```

```console
cat: decoys/.aws/credentials: Permission denied
```

```bash
uv run python nono_agent.py -- curl -sS --max-time 5 https://example.com/
```

```console
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: example.com
```

A seccomp filter on `connect` gives the same `curl: (6)` from the opposite direction: that filter says no to a syscall number, and this sandbox says the destination was never there.

## Cleanup

_~2 min · Hands-on_

Stop the containers and remove the profile and outputs:

```bash
docker compose --profile obi down -v
rm -f ~/.config/nono/profiles/agent.jsonc
rm -rf policies/rendered
rm -f workspace/notes.txt tetra.out tetra-enforce.out agent-enforce.out agent-override.out agent-nono.out agent-nono-profile.out collector.log obi.log dry-run.txt
```
